description: We are a team of software engineers and builders united by a shared interest in turning ideas into real, working products. Our core passions lie at the intersection of software engineering, artificial intelligence, and web development. We enjoy tackling technically challenging problems and delivering clean, scalable solutions that users can actually interact with.
summary:
Our team selected NASA’s “Harmonization of MODIS and VIIRS Hot Spots” challenge and developed FireLens, an interactive web application that combines satellite fire detections into a consistent historical record.

MODIS and VIIRS differ in resolution, sensitivity, and observation schedules, making direct comparisons unreliable. FireLens addresses this through a transparent harmonization pipeline that processes NASA FIRMS data, aligns detections spatially and temporally, and adjusts sensor-specific biases.

Using PostgreSQL/PostGIS, FastAPI, and Next.js, FireLens provides an interactive map and Burning Activity Calendar. Users can explore historical fire activity, identify seasonal patterns, compare observations with historical baselines, detect anomalies, and export results.

Our goal is to support emergency responders, researchers, and decision-makers with reliable historical fire information for better analysis and resource planning.

FireLens focuses on historical analysis rather than fire prediction, emphasizing transparency, validation, and uncertainty assessment. During the hackathon, we aim to deliver a functional MVP demonstrating the complete workflow from NASA satellite data to an accessible, user-friendly dashboard.
details:
FireLens – Project Details

FireLens is an interactive web application developed for NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026 to address the “Harmonization of MODIS and VIIRS Hot Spots” challenge. It transforms satellite fire detection records from NASA FIRMS into a unified, comparable historical dataset.

How It Works

FireLens processes MODIS and VIIRS hotspot data through a harmonization pipeline that filters detections, standardizes spatial and temporal information, and accounts for differences in sensor sensitivity and resolution. The processed data is stored in a geospatial database and presented through an interactive dashboard.

Users can:

  • Explore historical fire activity on an interactive map.
  • View a Burning Activity Calendar to identify seasonal trends.
  • Compare fire activity against historical averages.
  • Identify unusual activity through anomaly analysis.
  • Export data as CSV for further research.

Technologies Used

  • Frontend: Next.js, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, React-Leaflet, and Recharts.
  • Backend: Python and FastAPI.
  • Database: PostgreSQL, PostGIS, and Supabase.
  • Data Processing: Python, Pandas, and geospatial analysis tools.
  • Data Sources: NASA FIRMS (MODIS and VIIRS).
  • Collaboration: GitHub and Discord.

Creativity and Innovation

Rather than simply displaying satellite hotspots, FireLens transforms observations from different sensors into a consistent historical perspective. Its combination of sensor harmonization, interactive geospatial visualization, seasonal analysis, and anomaly detection makes complex satellite data easier to interpret.

Intended Impact

FireLens aims to help researchers, emergency responders, and decision-makers understand historical fire patterns, support resource planning, and improve environmental monitoring.

Key Considerations

Our team prioritized data reliability, transparency, sensor differences, geographic accuracy, usability, and scalability. We also considered the limited hackathon development time and focused on delivering a functional end-to-end solution.

FireLens does not predict future fires. Instead, it provides an accessible, data-driven foundation for understanding historical burning activity and identifying meaningful changes over time.
